Read more Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday as his first international visitor since becoming Prime Minister. The new PM said UK support for Ukraine “remains unwavering” ahead of the visit on Monday, just a week after entering Downing Street. They will visit a naval base where Mr Burnham will announce that Britain will hand over the intellectual property behind its new “Stone Cloak” electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale. The tablet-sized device is designed to block Russian detection of any drones it is fitted to. The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the jammers to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations. open image in gallery A firefighter walks at the site of a petrol station hit by a Russian airstrike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Zaporizhzhia ( Reuters ) Mr Burnham said in a statement: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. “Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve and we will not back down until we achieve long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine. “Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.” What is ‘Stone Cloak’? Following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology is expected to be incorporated into the UK’s next generation of long-range strike weapons, including Project Brakestop, the Government’s initiative to develop low-cost cruise missiles. During the visit, the two leaders will meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the past three weeks in the UK taking part in Exercise Sea Breeze, aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea. The new Prime Minister spoke to Mr Zelensky in one of his first calls after taking office last Monday and invited the Ukrainian leader to visit “at the earliest opportunity”. Mr Burnham, who has little foreign policy experience from his previous time in government, had vowed to maintain his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer’s resolute support for Ukraine before entering No 10. Sir Keir visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader. open image in gallery Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky pay their respects at a wreath laying at the Wall of Remembrance of the Fallen for Ukraine (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire ) On Sunday Romania shot down a suspected Russian drone after it crossed into its airspace — the third such incursion in three days in the Eastern European nation that's both a European Union and a NATO member, the country's president said. Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets scrambled from the Fete*ti airbase, under NATO's operational command, and shot down the drone over the Black Sea, the military alliance said. "A new drone was shot down this morning, at 10:13, by an F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force, over the territorial waters of Romania, in the Sulina-Chilia area," Romanian President Nicusor Dan said. He added that authorities found that one of the earlier intercepted drones appears to be "a Shahed type, used by the Russian Federation in the war of aggression against Ukraine. "This is the fourth recent downing by Romania of a drone violating NATO airspace in coordination with the alliance, said Col. Martin O'Donnell, a spokesperson for NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe, known as SHAPE.Before the last three interceptions, Romanian jets shot down a drone in the sky above Estonia in May, he said. Romanian pilots and planes are based in Lithuania from where they have broad strike capabilities as part of NATO's force posture. "As we continue to prove, NATO is constantly on the watch and prepared to defend itself from any threat," O'Donnell said. Beállítom The Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has issued a response to the statement adopted by the Ukrainian parliament on Thursday. The Ukrainian resolution condemns the atrocities committed against Hungarians in Transcarpathia during and after World War II, and is an important gesture toward Hungary, which is still blocking Ukraine’s EU accession process. In a statement released on Friday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its gratitude for Ukraine’s move. “Today’s decision by the Ukrainian parliament is a fitting tribute to the memory of the victims and an important step towards confronting the Soviet past and uncovering the truth about these events", the statement reads. They added that Hungary also strongly condemns all forms of ethnic discrimination and persecution and stands ready to cooperate both in uncovering the past and in honoring the memory of the victims. The Ukrainian parliament adopted the statement on Thursday without any votes against; in it, Ukraine officially recognizes and condemns the crimes committed by the Soviet military administration in Transcarpathia between 1944 and 1946. According to the statement, Ukraine, “as a democratic state that recognizes the rule of law and condemns all manifestations of totalitarianism, considers it its duty to officially acknowledge the fact of the mass repression committed by the Soviet military administration against the civilian population of Hungarian nationality between 1944 and 1946, known as “malenykij robot,” as well as the oppression committed against the ethnic German population of Transcarpathia, and considers these crimes committed by the totalitarian communist regime.” The declaration states that memorial plaques will be erected, academic research will be organized, and educational programs will be implemented in honor of the victims of Soviet oppression in Transcarpathia. As we reported on Thursday, Ukraine’s EU accession process has been stalled because Hungary continues to block the screening reports for negotiation clusters 2 and 3. Regarding this, Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Orbán said that they do not support Ukraine’s fast-track accession under any circumstances, and are now waiting for the Ukrainians to implement the agreement on the rights of the Hungarian minority negotiated in June. As she said, the Ukrainian parliament must adopt the legislative amendments which guarantee the rights of the Hungarian minority in the areas of education, culture, and political representation. The agreement concerning the Hungarian minority in Ukraine was a prerequisite for Hungary consenting to the launch of Cluster I, and if the legislative amendments to which Ukraine has committed do not take place in 2026 and 2027, the implementation of Cluster I will automatically be halted. https://www.politico.eu/article/five-eu-.text: Mette Frederiksen is prime minister of Denmark. Friedrich Merz is chancellor of Germany. Rob Jetten is prime minister of the Netherlands. Christian Stocker is chancellor of Austria. Petteri Orpo is prime minister of Finland. In a more dangerous and uncertain world, a strong Europe must be ready to make bold choices. In a world of real fiscal constraints, Europe cannot fund new priorities by simply adding them to old ones. We must make choices. Europe’s next long-term budget is about much more than money. It’s about political priorities. The next Multiannual Financial Framework will determine how Europe spends its common resources well into the next decade. Advertisement Advertisement Budgets are where political priorities become real. Speeches, declarations and summit conclusions matter, but ultimately it is the allocation of money that reveals what governments are genuinely prepared to prioritize. Europe needs to become more competitive, more sovereign and better able to defend itself. There is no other choice. Our budget must reflect that new reality. The status quo of the current MFF cannot be the starting point. It is too focused on subsidies and transfers allocated largely in advance, leaving too little room for what Europe urgently needs: common investment in security and defense, competitiveness, innovation, and the fight against irregular migration. The next MFF will be the test of whether Europe has understood the message of Mario Draghi’s landmark report on European competitiveness. It will show whether our promises of more common European investment are real — or just rhetoric. Mario Draghi addresses the audience during the conference ‘One Year After the Draghi Report’ at the EU Charlemagne building on September 16, 2025 in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images That requires choices. And choices require political courage. This does not mean abandoning traditional policies, but we cannot just add every new priority to every old one and send the bill to taxpayers. Almost every EU member country is making painful efforts to consolidate its public finances. Those that are not should concern us even more. There will be no European sovereignty without sound public finances. We are doing our part: The group of net contributors that recently met in Berlin stands for almost 40% of the financing of the EU budget and provides around 70% of EU member countries’ bilateral support for Ukraine. We are investing heavily in our common security and defense. We are not tight-fisted. Nor are we hiding behind the label “frugal.” In fact, when it comes to supporting Ukraine, greater engagement by other member states is both reasonable and urgently needed. Advertisement Advertisement We are not calling for cuts compared to the existing MFF. The MFF will grow to address our strategic priorities. Any such increase during a period of domestic fiscal consolidation is already a significant commitment. It shows how seriously we take the need for a stronger Europe. But we also need to be realistic. The European Commission has proposed a nominal increase of around 60%. That is simply not realistic. Not economically, not politically and certainly not at a time when public finances in several member countries are a cause for serious concern. This is why we call for a balanced cut to the Commission’s proposal of several hundred billion euros. In times when we are reducing staffing levels, we expect the EU institutions to operate with the staff they have today. There can be no increase. The EU budget is ultimately paid for by European citizens. That remains true whatever financing mechanism we invent. So, there is no avoiding the difficult question of the overall volume. Common borrowing cannot be the answer either: The debt taken on during the pandemic will already burden the next MFF by almost €170 billion. That money is no longer available for our new priorities. Much of the cost consists of interest payments that must be made regardless of when the principal is repaid. Postponing repayment does little to solve the financing equation. It should be self-evident to everyone that respect for our common values and the rule of law are indispensable preconditions to any European funding. The world around us has changed, our common priorities have, and our common budget must too. It is the only way to build a strong Europe that is fit for the future. Advertisement Advertisement
